utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Could the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kijac. Please be seated, and make yourself comfortable. Before you make -- before you commence your evidence, Mr. Kijac, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Kijac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Minister. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please come closer to the microphone, speak slowly and respond verbally to everything so that it can be recorded. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up in e-court, please, 1D9592.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that statement on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read and sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the last page, please, so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this statement faithfully reflect what you have stated to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the same questions today, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Essentially, certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I tender this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the admission of the statement, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the associated exhibits, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There are 17 associated exhibits being offered, all are on our 65 ter list except for 1D09529, which we would ask be added to our 65 ter list as we decided to use it after that list had been prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber was not able to view that document because it was not uploaded on to e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it was actually sent by e-mail over the weekend as part of our package of materials, but the ITSS people didn't upload it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it should be led live.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And there seems to be two translations for 1D9826. Could you identify which is the correct one. Shall we upload it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am only seeing one translation in e-court for -- in my e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's leave it. And 1D9834, referred to in paragraph 12, the Chamber is of the view that it does not form part -- an inseparable or indispensable part of the statement. Further, the Chamber is not satisfied with its provenance so it will not be admitted. And 65 ter 18453 referred to in para 37, the Chamber will admit only article 8 of the document, out of 64 pages. Otherwise, Ms. Pack, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Nothing to add, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Except 1D9529 and 1D9834, all the other associated exhibits will be admitted into evidence and be assigned numbers by the Registry in due course. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we give the exhibit number for the statement at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit D4143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should now like to read a brief summary of the statement of Mr. Dragan Kijac in the English language. [In English] Dragan Kijac began his career in state security in 1983 when he was appointed inspector and supervisor for the republican Secretariat of the Interior, State Security Service for Yugoslavia. When the war broke out in 1992, Dragan Kijac was appointed chief of the Sarajevo National Security Service sector of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He later became the head of the State Security Service of Republika Srpska Ministry of Interior and was serving in his capacity at the time of the Srebrenica events in July 1995. Dragan Kijac later served as minister for -- of the interior in the Republika Srpska government and deputy prime minister. In July 1995, on 12 July 1995, Dragan Kijac became aware that after the fall of Srebrenica, the Army of Republika Srpska had captured Ibran Mustafic, a former deputy in the BH assembly and high-ranking SDA official. He ordered the chief of the Bijeljina State Security Service to take custody of Mr. Mustafic and transfer him to the collection camp in Bijeljina for interrogation. Mr. Mustafic was transported and interrogated by the State Security Service and remains alive to this day. In the morning of 14th of July, 1995, Mr. Kijac travelled to Montenegro for the wedding of his deputy. He returned to Pale in the evening of 18th of July. On 19th of July, he met with President Karadzic in Pale. The subject of the meeting was likely the preparation for President Karadzic's upcoming travel. Mr. Kijac did not know about the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica when he met with President Karadzic. Mr. Kijac did not see any report from any organ including the military intelligence service which indicated that prisoners from Srebrenica had been executed. Mr. Kijac never informed President Karadzic about the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica, nor did President Karadzic ever give any indication during their meetings that he was aware that the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica had taken place. Mr. Kijac believes that had President Karadzic known about such crimes, he would have acted to prevent and/or punish the perpetrators. And I have only one question for one document. I will not lead live documents that are not admitted for the sake of saving time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kijac, I wanted to ask you were you with me in Krajina, in Banja Luka, in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what kind of relationship existed at that time between the civilian authorities, including me, with the commanders of our army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Briefly, they were not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did ever information reach you that certain services acted unlawfully vis-a-vis the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. I realised that later. There were certain documents where you were a target of their interest, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness 1D09525? We have a translation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber what kind of document is this, or what is this JUDA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: This is an intelligence report produced by the military intelligence service and it concerns an operative action called JUDA, J-U-D-A, and it says the source is called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear what the source is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Briefly, you were a target of the military intelligence services interest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat as to its source? The interpreters couldn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source is "Klej," I can see at the top of the page, "Klej" written as K-l-e-j, and it says strictly confidential a number and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all your knowledge of the law, could you tell us from the legal point of view, how would you qualify this treatment of the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: This is absolutely unlawful. It should never happen that a state service should keep the president under surveillance. This report shows that all your communications, contacts, meetings, were under surveillance from dusk till dawn. This particular report covers one entire day, from dawn until the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this the only document of its kind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I had occasion to see three or four similar documents in my work with the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4159, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. At this moment, I have no further questions for Mr. Kijac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. As you have noted, Mr. Kijac, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is through your written statement. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll start with your time as head of the DB, Mr. Kijac. Paragraph 9 of your statement, you don't need to look at it, you describe yourself as a professional, whose achievements in the DB were remarkable, yes? Yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: This assessment was made by my superiors, not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This was a specialised service, expert in gathering information and distributing it; right? That's the heart of what you did.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, I started working after moving to the State Security Service from the Court as an operative worker, the lowest category of the operative worker. That's the lowest title, inspector.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Kijac, we don't need the detail. I'm just talking to you about your time as head of the DB. I just asked you a question about the DB service, expert in gathering information and distributing it, that's the heart of what you did, is that right, accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You reported, as head of the DB to the minister of the interior and in July 1995, you reported to Kovac; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: He was your superior, your boss, in the MUP in July 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: That's correct. He was deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Staying with 1995, you reported to the president directly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were obliged to brief him broadly on the security situation in the RS, to keep the president informed; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You reported to him in writing and orally; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Mainly in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, you met with the president in 1995, let's just -- 1995 you met with him or you spoke to him on a weekly basis, that's what is recorded in his diary. You'd agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: It doesn't necessarily mean reporting. Reports are made in writing. We can discuss written reports but the reporting was done mainly in writing. If you look at the progress reports, you will see that President Karadzic received, let's say, a thousand briefs per year and the reports were made in writing. We were able to discuss different situations verbally but the reporting was done in writing, and my service would prepare all the information, make a selection and produce reports to the prime minister, the president, et cetera, always in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. You discussed different situations with him verbally. You reported verbally, you communicated with him verbally, about the situation, the security situation in the country, right, you don't disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. We commented on various things that reached the president in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Of course, you met with him and spoke with him on more occasions than is recorded in his diary, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I don't know what's recorded in the diary. I did not follow that and I can't say, but we met very often, certainly four or five times per month, sometimes more often.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You personally reported as necessary to other organs of state, the VRS, the president of the assembly, the prime minister; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I was not answerable to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: All the way through the war, the DB, you, shared information with and received information from the VRS, you'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. But that doesn't mean that I was answerable to the Army of Republika Srpska. It is the case that we shared information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Fine. You shared information with them as necessary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which was necessary, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The question was you shared information with them as necessary, I'm sorry, it got left out of the -- I -- I interrupted and it got left out of the transcript. I think the answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You nodded, yes? You have to make sure that you answer --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We will go to P05557, please. This is a report that you wrote in April 1993, it's a report on the work of the DB in 1992, throughout the course of 1992. We have the translation. Recognise this report; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We will go to page 4, please, 4 in the English, 4 in the B/C/S. Look at the paragraph, please, begins -- in English it begins preceding from this pre-war intelligence and it goes on to talk about your activities during the war. I'd just like to ask you about the last two sentences. You're talking about the information that you obtained during the war and you can perhaps see these two sentences I'm going to read in English. This information was continuously passed on to the state and military organs which based their further activities among other things on it as well. It's at the bottom of the first paragraph in English. The service co-operated with other organs engaged in these tasks, usually military organs, exchanging daily the information that had been collected. Using this they could correct and redirect the further course of our interests more in keeping with current events. And then you go on to describe in the following paragraph the methods used to collect information, the service came by such data by using different kinds of operative and operative technical resources and methods, the most frequent of these were interviews with captured enemy soldiers, Serbs who had been exchanged or came out of territory under enemy control, and others who in various ways were in a position to come by interesting data, and it goes on. So that's -- accurately describes, isn't it -- doesn't it, that the use of information provided by the DB to correct and redirect the activities of the VRS and MUP units; right? You ensured they had accurate information upon which to base their activities, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that part was not displayed for me here. I would like to read that, although I quite understand what you're saying, but could you please find that page and tell me which paragraph it is, if possible?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. We can hardly hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not see on page 2 which I have displayed in front of me what you read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Goes on to page 5. You can go on to page 5. At the bottom of the page it's -- in the e-court it's page 4. I think we have -- going over to page 5, continues to describe the methods used. So it was the bottom of the preceding page you were looking at and now going on to the top of this page 5, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: And we are in page 3, and it is my understanding that you said page 5, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Don't worry about what I'm saying to the Registrar. What I'm talking about is a page within the system here. You're looking at the right page, page 3, right. You were looking at pages 2 and 3 in this copy here. That's what you -- what I read out --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. If it's this part here that's what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Got it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Do you remember my question? I'll repeat it. Information provided by the DB was used to correct and redirect the activities of the VRS and the MUP, MUP units you ensured, didn't you, that civilian and military organs had accurate information upon which to base their activities, that's right, isn't it, and that's what you say here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, basically yes, but I have to point something else out. What comes from the field, the military part goes to the military, and the police part is redirected to the police, because we were not a database to collect information for ourselves. We collected what we got and sent that on to the police or the military. That is not to say that our information was supposed to be corrected. Perhaps their information was better and more correct than ours, but we sent that to those organs so that they could correct through their own analysis the overall knowledge acquired from the ground. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I asked you about the methods used to obtain information, it's the following paragraph, interviewing POWs, that was an important source, wasn't it, of information for you in the DB, yes? You can say yes rather than nod, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Partly, yes. But basic information, we got from the population that were refugees. We had access to POWs only where we had an interest to talk to them. POWs were under the VRS, they were never under our jurisdiction, and we did not have any detention facilities. So it's only where the State Security Service showed a certain interest for a particular person, name and surname, they could go and ask in writing for approval to speak to such persons about things that the State Security Service was interested in and nothing more than that. That is to say we did not have any POWs of our own. We did not have wide-ranging discussions with POWs. We only asked about things that we were interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I haven't asked a question. What's the objection? To the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an objection to the answer. It is not correct that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, you cannot object to the answer. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not to the answer, to the question. It is not correct that the question only had to do with methods. There is something else stated in 11 rather than what it says in 22 and 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That is not an appropriate objection. It wasn't raised when I asked the question and it's, in truth, an objection to the answer. Entirely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I wasn't suggesting to you that POWs were in your jurisdiction. You gave me a long answer and I think the short answer to my question that POWs were an important source of information for you was yes; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: POWs were not an important source of our information because we only talked to certain individuals where the State Security Service had a particular interest, so that would not be a broad spectrum. It's not that you'd walk into a military prison and that you would talk to all the persons there, as far as I know, from the State Security Service in Bijeljina, that was a big prison, Batkovic. Our operatives, I don't know whether they went there once or twice to interview people throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's just go to the following page, please, of this document, in the English page 8 of e-court, please, and page 12 in the B/C/S in e-court just to finish off.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you can see it's the second paragraph in the English I'm going to look at, and in the B/C/S you can see it's the long paragraph. So you describe in summary the data collected by the SMB, you say it's distributed in a timely fashion throughout the year - I'm paraphrasing - to the responsible state and military organs who used it as a basis for planning direction of their activity, making evaluations, and so on: "Continuous exchanges," and here I'm quoting, "of information with the intelligence and security organs of the VRS were especially fruitful with among other things 1.085 written reports sent to them." You go on: "A significant," the following sentence, "equally significant attention was devoted to informing the responsible state organs." You go on, and then just further down: "It should be emphasised that priority is given to the timely and ongoing distribution of information and practically not a single piece of information ended up for internal SMB use." So you are there accurately stating in your report in 1993 that your priority was to obtain and distribute information, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The information that was received from the ground was analysed at department level and then depending on the segments that were usable, they were sent on further, if that could be my answer. So all information of a military nature were ceded to the military and then it says here, I think, 1.085 pieces of information. So about commanders, weapons, possible axes of attack, all of that was ceded to military security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. We will go to July 1995, please. You talk in your statement at paragraph 49 about the Bijeljina CRDB, the centre, the DB centre in Bijeljina, which received information, didn't it, from the Zvornik DB branch? You don't need to look at your statement to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Goran Radovic was head of the CRDB in Bijeljina; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mile Renovica was head of the Zvornik DB branch; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could you get a little closer to the microphone and speak more clearly, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. Mile Renovica was head of the department in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: He had operatives working under him. They included Sinisa Glogovac, Aleksandar Todorovic, Vitomir Tomic. These are all DB operatives working under Renovica; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes, but these first two names that you mentioned were active duty personnel in the security service; whereas the third person, Mr. Tomic was a reserve person, so he was not a professional. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The others are professional DB operatives, Todorovic, Glogovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: They were permanently employed, but if we look at the operatives in Zvornik, there were seven or eight of them there. Only two of them were experienced operatives, or rather, operatives before the war as well. All the rest were taken in during the war in 1993, 1994, whereas Sinisa Glogovac and Mile Renovica were pre-war operatives of the state security, and by the same token I would say that they were trained to collect information on the ground because to create a young operative during the course of a single year only is quite impossible. If you take into account the fact that after I got my law degree and after working in the judiciary for a year and a half, I came as an intern and I could not do anything for a year at the State Security Service; that is to say, I was just learning the tools of the trade because that was the prevalent practice at the time, that it was only after one year that I could do anything on my own, independently.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Sinisa Glogovac, your professional, was territorially responsible for the Bratunac area; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, the service had this territorial organisation and although he lived in Zvornik, he covered the territory of Srebrenica, or rather, the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In July 1995, the reporting chain from operative to you and up was working, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: What do you mean from you and up? From operative Glogovac to me, if that's what you meant? I did not quite understand you. You say from you and up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I said the reporting chain from the operative to you was working, wasn't it, I'll break it down, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you were reporting up, right, up to Kovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were distributing the information you received to Kovac, to the president, to Karisik, to the VRS security organs, right, to your counterpart Karisik in the Public Security Service and to the VRS security organs; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Right. Daily information was sent to the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say to Mr. Karisik and the deputy minister, Mr. Kovac, while the information that had to do with the military, with the Army of Republika Srpska, was sent to Mr. Tolimir. Part of the information that was used from this information that came in was sent to the president of the republic, to the prime minister and the speaker of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You sent reports, didn't you, about the Srebrenica area in July, as you described to Kovac, to Karisik and so on. You were sending these reports on the 11, 12, 13 July; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You've now come here today with an alibi for the 14th to the 18th of July when the killings were going on. You were at a wedding in Montenegro, is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, that's not an alibi. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, DB operatives were interrogating prisoners in the white house in Potocari; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No, according to my information. According to Mr. Sinisa Glogovac's statement and Mr. Mile Renovica's statement, I had an opportunity to see that. No one interviewed anyone at the "white house." Only two or three interviews were conducted at the public security station in Bratunac in an office, and the public security station gave that office to our operatives for a few days. However, there was a lot of commotion at this station after two or three interviews our people gave up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to ask you about Potocari, not asking you about statements from Renovica and so on. They haven't testified in this case. P0438.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No, you asked about the white house. I don't know where the white house is, but there is mention of the white house in both statements and it says there that no interviews were conducted, and you asked me about interviews. To the best of my understanding, that's how I understood the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not asking about what you've read in other people's interviews, okay? I'm asking you about Potocari, so just confine yourself to what you know and we'll look at some documents. P04388, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. This is a communication, Popovic, and I'm going to ask you -- it's dated the 12th of July, 1730 hours. At the top you can see the time stamped at the top, if you look at page 2, please, in the English and it's the bottom paragraph in B/C/S. He says, paragraph 3, we are -- he's describing what's going on in Potocari, and he says: We are separating men from 17 to 60 years of age and we are not transporting them. We have about 70 of them so far and the security organs and the DB state security are working with them. State security operatives are interrogating men in the white house in Potocari, aren't they, with Drina Corps security, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, you see, first of all, I mean, as far as I can see, this is a military document. I cannot speak about a military document. If I do not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters did not understand the end of the sentence. Interpreter's note: We cannot understand the witness or hear him. We are sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kijac, could you come closer to the microphone? And then speak slowly and please repeat your answer. The interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and do I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, could you shut -- yes. Now, please repeat again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a military document and I cannot speak about it. I can only say that in Potocari, we had one operative, possibly two, who did not take part in what is referred to in this third paragraph because physically one or two persons cannot take part in that. How can one or two persons separate people? Somebody else had to do that. Also I'm saying that both of them in their statements -- Mr. Sinisa Glogovac said that they did not conduct any interviews together with the Army of Republika Srpska in relation to the POWs. That they only conducted a few interviews at the public security station in Bratunac and because the conditions were impossible for conducting interviews they gave up on this measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This document does not say that DB members, operatives, are separating the men from the group. But they are just participating. Could you read the last two sentences again, so whether you agree with this report --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can. They did not take part in the interviews, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I ask? I mean, I cannot find this, that this was done at the white house. This work with the prisoners that has to do with the white house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was a question from Ms. Pack. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You say in your statement at paragraph 50 - don't need to look at it - you ordered your agent in Srebrenica be found and taken to a safe location. He was in Potocari, wasn't he? Your agent, DB agent? He was removed from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I don't know where he was. We had a contact in Potocari during the war. I gave orders to have him found and evacuated to a safe location. I really do not know, I don't have any details about that, where he was found or anything like that. At any rate, the report that I received was that he was transported to a safe location.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 11, the witness said: I don't know whether he was in Potocari, we had a contact in Srebrenica during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Kijac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't know where they found him. During the war, we had this agent in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So you're denying that your operatives were interviewing prisoners in Potocari. You don't deny, do you, that your operatives were present in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I do not deny that they were present. I mean, I don't know about locations, but I'm not denying that our operatives had interviews conducted at the Bratunac public security station. As far as I know, in Potocari our operatives did not conduct any interview with these persons. There are no documents to that effect either.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You are aware, aren't you, that Borovcanin testified for the accused here on the 7th of June that he received information from DB operatives Vito Tomic and Sinisa Glogovac. You received information from them on the 12th of July in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Please, if possible, could the volume be adjusted? My hearing is not very good at all. So could you please put the question to me again? And I seem to be having trouble with my headphones too. They keep falling off. Could you please put the question again?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Borovcanin testified for the accused here on the 7th of June, and he said that he received information from DB operatives Vito Tomic and Sinisa Glogovac on the 12th of July in Potocari. What do you have to say about that? You'd accept that that's what happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he received that, but I can say that that would have been the normal thing to do, that our operatives would give information.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's to say I would not deny that. I cannot confirm that either. They are the only ones who know. But I can say that operatives of the state security who operated in the area were - how do I put this? - duty-bound to send this information, or rather, give it on the spot to police or military organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So you don't deny now that your operatives in Potocari were gathering information, passing it on to Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, you're going back to Potocari and I'm speaking in general terms. I, as the chief of the service, do not know whether an operative collected information in Bratunac or in Potocari or wherever, but as far as I know, they did not take part in collecting information, intelligence, from persons in Potocari. They collected information and I repeat once again only on one or two occasions they had these very brief interviews at the public security station at Bratunac, and probably that is the information that they gave to -- it doesn't matter -- Borovcanin or whoever was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could we see P4939, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is a document sent by you in the late evening hours on the 12th of July to Kovac and to Karisik. You offer detailed information on the movement of the column in the first paragraph, there you can see that, don't need to read it to you, and then at the bottom, still on the B/C/S page 1, in the English page 1, bottom paragraph, going over to the following page 2, you talk about the agreement to evacuate civilians from Potocari that you say has been reached. And then you say: The evacuation was suspended at night and will - going over the page in the English - resume on the morning of the 13th of July. It should be noted that among the people staying in Potocari, there are hardly any men fit for fighting. So you are reporting there information from your operatives who have been interrogating prisoners in Potocari; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I have to tell you again you are insisting on Potocari but I keep saying that to the best of my knowledge, our men did not participate in any interviews in Potocari, but at the public security station in Bratunac. We are running in circles here. You're asking me the same question and I believe that I have answered that question already. But I can explain. According to what I know, our two operatives who were there conducted interviews with three or four prisoners at the public security station in Bratunac and after they saw that there were no conditions for normal conducting of interviews, they suspended all interviews with prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's look at P04389, please. P04389.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is another communication from you to Kovac and Karisik. This is dated the 13th of July. You report in the first paragraph on the capture of a large number of Muslim soldiers, over 300 of them, in ambushes. Going down that first paragraph, you talk about the movement of the Muslim men and you say this is been confirmed many times in interviews with prisoners. Going down, you talk about Mustafic - we will get back to that later - among the prisoners. He can be a great opponent of Oric and can be, with the necessary preparation, used well in the media. You've spoken about that, we'll come back to it. So you report that during the night of the 12th/13th of July, 1995, members of the VRS and MUP managed to capture a large number of Muslim soldiers in ambushes; right? You confirm information on the movement of the column many times in interviews with prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So you -- you're interrogating prisoners, you were tracking the movement of the Muslim column, and you were reporting that information up the chain, yeah?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, you see, this information came from the Bijeljina centre. I cannot say at this point whether this was an interview or whether this was indirectly obtained data from the policemen or from the soldiers who participated in the action, as you keep insisting on interviews, and I say that it is quite normal that every service conducts interviews with POWs. But according to my knowledge, our men did not do that because we only had two people, two men, there. How could two men conduct interviews with 300 POWs? That is impossible. They couldn't even take their basic particulars, let alone any more extensive interviews. In the hills, in the woods --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You tell us in paragraph 50 of your statement that Ibran Mustafic from 12th of July -- you say you ordered Radovic to take him over and transfer him to Bijeljina; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was transferred to Bijeljina. I don't know whether it was on the 12th or the 13th. The moment we found out, we were informed at Pale, that there existed information to the effect that Ibran Mustafic was among the prisoners. We agreed, i.e., I ordered to the Bijeljina centre that Ibran Mustafic should be transferred to Bijeljina. As far as I know, that was done. This was the chief of the Bijeljina centre with a group of people was in charge of this operation, as he was taken out of a group of prisoners and transferred to Bijeljina and the interview was continued there in respect of the facts that we were interested in. We were interested in only individuals, not prisoners of war generally, only individuals, if they were of any interest to the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You pulled him out of -- the DB pulled him out of the hangar behind the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac on the night of the 12th/13th July, right, that's where he was detained?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I don't know that, believe me, I don't know that. I don't have that information. The only information that I have --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. You don't have that information. That's the evidence in this case, that he was called out of the hangar behind the Vuk Karadzic school and that is from P03940. He was identified by you as of sufficiently high value to save; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, this is actually demeaning. This is not a fair question. What do you mean save? This is not correct. Yes, we took him in order to extract certain information from him that we were interested in. Save from whom? What do you mean by save?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, he -- he was an opponent, wasn't he, of Naser Oric? You identified him as a high value prisoner. You told us that, right, yes, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, he was a person of security-related interest to us, that is unquestionable and that is why and in view of the position that he held prior to the war as a deputy, he was unquestionably of interest to the service. And that is why, along those lines, so to speak, we actually extracted him from wherever he was and we took him to Bijeljina in order to conduct interviews with him to shed some more light on the things which were happening in the area of Srebrenica in 1991 and 1992 and probably statements of Mr. Ibran Mustafic exist about that, as well as statements about the conduct of our operatives and statements about what he had said to us, but I do not agree with the term which you used which is to save. What was he saved from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the exact reference? This P3940 is a transcript, if -- where is this exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was the question put by Ms. Pack. You do not interrupt her question. She was putting her case to the witness and the witness properly answered the question. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: What do I mean what was he saved from, Mr. Kijac? What do I mean? You had it within your power, didn't you, to save those Muslim men whom you considered to be useful to you, valuable to the DB. And on the night of the 12th July you did so because you knew that the POWs were going to be killed; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: That is not right, Your Honours. I just answered that question. We saved no one. We pursued our own interests. Our interest was to extract a person which was of interest to the security service from -- on a security-related basis, so there was no plan, there was no knowledge about the liquidation, as you're trying to impute to me right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, so you say, Mr. Kijac, you tell us in your statement at paragraph 55 that you didn't have information until the end of the year 2000, when all the media began to report it. That's right? The year 2000, you had no information about the killings. Is that your evidence, your honest evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Precisely, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you talk about paragraph 56 you were shown some communications that were sent to you personally and to the president from the VRS security organs on 14, 15, 16, 17 July, you refer to those in your statement paragraph 56, they are missing. You're aware of that, those communications are missing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Which paragraph did you say that was?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Paragraph 56. You talk about some communications that are logged.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, now I see. As I have already said, we exchanged information with a military intelligence agency. You saw for yourself that we sent daily reports to them and they sent to us, as a rule, integral intelligence reports associated with a situation on the battlefield. I was shown here by Mr. Karadzic's team that the 14th, 15th, 16th, and 17th of July, four intelligence reports were sent to the DB, to me, which ostensibly do not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: They are missing. Not --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I've said here, so when I returned, this happened at a time when I was not at Pale. So upon my return had anything important been contained in those reports, my chiefs of departments would have at the time imparted that information to me for my consideration. Usually when I returned from a trip, and this was another trip, it had to do with the wedding of my deputy, but there were other trips when I went to the different regions for different meetings in the republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Didn't know anything until 2000 when the media began to report it. You, head of the DB, you were aware, weren't you, of -- and you followed international news media and UN reporting during the Srebrenica operations, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: As I have said already, I didn't know anything until the year 2000 nor did a single paper coming to the DB which would indicate that something was happening with the POWs. On the other hand, I have to stress that the POW -- that POWs are not within the jurisdiction of the State Security Service. It is not a sort of a supervisor --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not talking about jurisdiction. You don't need to hide behind the law. I'm asking you about what you knew, okay? You don't need to keep on going back to jurisdiction. Let me ask you about what you knew, okay? Listen. You are aware, aren't you, that by the 17th of July international news media were reporting that thousands, thousands, of terrified people had been deported from the enclave and that men of fighting age had been taken away for screening? You were aware of news reports to that effect; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No. It's not right. First and foremost, I do not speak English. At that time we were not following the media so that we would be able to know what was happening on the 17th or on the 20th. We were living at Pale in a very specific milieu where often there was no electricity or no water, and it's not realistic when you refer to the world media in that context. What I'm saying is that we knew -- that we knew --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You, the head of the DB, weren't following the news media? Is that what you're saying? Is that your evidence, your honest evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were following the international -- the reporting of internationals; right? Or do you deny following UN reporting, ICRC reporting, all of the other international reporting at the time in July? You were aware of and followed that sort of reporting, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: We follow what we could follow, what we were equipped to follow. We did follow the UN system of communications. For instance, the Tuzla and Zagreb communication when they say that the Nordic Battalion had received about 30.000 refugees, we did manage to intercept some communications but you are talking about following the media. No, we didn't do that. We didn't have the requisite conditions for that. We did follow the activities of certain international organisations when we had a technical requirements fulfilled for that to be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay, we have moved on from the media. I'm asking you about international organisations, ICRC, the UN. You followed their reporting, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No. We were not that successful, as a matter of fact. Let me look at those reports. If I looked at them, perhaps I have seen them but do not remember them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the witness is following your question. There seems to be a translation issue. What did you mean by following the international reporting? Ms. Pack, you can put your question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were aware of and read international reporting, and here I'm talking about UN, ICRC, the reporting of international organisations, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Let me see a report that came to the state security department. Perhaps we have a misunderstanding here. If I can see one, I can tell you. Perhaps I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You intercepted, for example -- one example, you intercepted ICRC reporting, internal reporting of the ICRC, something you did in the DB, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: You must show me something. You must show me something. Generally speaking, what intercepting? Is there a single interview or conversation talk that you can tell me is an intercepted conversation, international organisations? There is one, I'm talking about Srebrenica. We intercepted a conversation between Tuzla and Zagreb. I believe it was on the 13th, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can answer the question in principle, can't you? You don't need to look at documents to answer the question in principle, whether you, the DB -- you, as a matter of practice, one of the methods by which you secured information was to obtain that information from international organisations, whether through their agents, whether through intercepting their communications. That was something you did; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you take a look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That is something that you did. You -- one of the means by which you obtained information in the DB was to get that information from international organisations, whether through communicating with their employees, their operatives, whether through intercepting their reporting, that is something you did to get information. You can agree with that, can't you, in principle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm not questioning what you're saying in that particular segment. The service does collect intelligence and information and from -- including from the foreign factor. We did collect information through a network of agents and through intercepting conversations, but at this point, I fail to see how do you believe that a service in war conditions when there is no electricity, when there are no generating sets, when there are no technical conditions, how we could have done that. How could I have seen what UNPROFOR was doing or any other international organisation in such conditions? You look at our papers, you will very frequently see -- but that is not what you are representing that to be. This is just some daily information which was gathered by very successful operatives who managed to infiltrate some international organisations and to obtain information which was of interest to us. But intercepted conversations were very infrequent. When we -- for instance, when we talk about the Bijeljina centre, the centre of the state security was not there before the war, and the -- ipso facto, it did not have the necessary equipment to actually cover the work in the bases there in Republika Srpska, if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were following the news media in Serbia, weren't you? You were aware of the Petrovic tape that was confiscated from studio 3 [sic] shortly after it was broadcast, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I hear of it. I don't know who Petrovic is at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You weren't following the Serbian news media?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No, very seldom. We followed our own media. Actually I don't know whether we had any official channels established with Serbia. I mean we at Pale.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. On page 32, it is line 10, where first it is stated no, and here on page 34 -- so on page 34, line 7, it is stated that they didn't have necessary equipment to actually cover the work in the bases there in Republika Srpska where it should say it is outside Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Shall we continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Sorry I misspoke, it's "Studio B," not "3."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So your evidence is -- your honest evidence today is that you were not aware of the content of the Serbian news media, right, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: We do not understand each other again or perhaps you're mistaken. Studio B is Belgrade studio and it can only be seen in the Belgrade area. Studio B is a Belgrade TV station and it can be seen, viewed, only in the Belgrade area. Your question was not properly formulated or you're mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: General question: Were you following the news media in Serbia, general question, answer yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No, no, no. We in Republika Srpska, to the best of my recollection, we did not receive any media signals from Serbia, for a while, that is, so that my -- my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] newspapers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 13610, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is a communication from you to the president of Republika Srpska, the accused, it's dated 21st of July, 1995, to the president personally. Just going to deal with bits of it. Broadly reports on the content of news reporting in Serbia and elsewhere in the region which you apparently in your bubble in Pale were able to access at the time; right? Let me just ask you to look, please, at the English page 3, I'm afraid -- just get the B/C/S reference for you. It's in page 2 of the B/C/S. Just look at that, shall we? Just above that heading, 1, general situation, ICRC activities, just before that, you say this, you say this to the president, please find attached a report by the ICRC for the period between 10 and 16 July 1995. That's a report you are attaching for the president from the ICRC; right? On the 21st of July, 1995, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Probably yes, that is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So you got reports from the ICRC, didn't you, and you passed them on to the president in July 1995; right? Yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, we misunderstand each other. Again, this is just one report, we are talking about one report. We did not have all reports. This is one report that was presented to the -- to the president because it was captured by our measures, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Look at what you say under paragraph 1, judging by the manner -- this is reporting on Belgrade media. Judging by the manner of reporting by the official media, the fall of Srebrenica and, in particular, the deportation of its population, seems to have happened on another planet, the "Politika" does not even acknowledge the transfer of 23.000 people. However, only a day before this dramatic event, the media were widely publishing an interview that Milosevic gave with "Tanjug," and it goes on. And on the following pages you talk about Pristina, an ethnic Albanian man dying on the 4th of July at his home in Podujevo, all sorts of details regarding the region, but silence about the content of that ICRC report, silence about Srebrenica in this written report. You don't comment on it, you don't need to, do you, because you all know what's going on; right? You all know what's going on after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I have to revert to the beginning again. We didn't know at that time what was going on in Srebrenica. This was obviously submitted by regional security centre, state security centre. This is not the picture that Pale had. This could be Bijeljina because they were nearer Serbia, and they had the opportunity to have the daily press survey [indiscernible] Serbian signal. So this is information submitted to us by the regional centre and we just took it over because we did not generate information. We at the top do not generate information. We just receive it. And then what we receive we translate into a report of this type. So I reiterate: We did not have this picture at Pale, nor did we have any reports from the Serbian media. We could not follow the Serbian media. We didn't have any media from Serbia. Perhaps they did come to Banja Luka, I don't know that, at this point, but at Pale, I didn't receive a single written media from Serbia during the war, nor was I able to follow their TV programmes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Not talking about Serbian Belgrade TV. I'm not asking you about Belgrade TV. This is a document you signed; right? You signed this document. Your signature is on the last page. Seen you've seen that; right? Can we have the last page of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. It's not in dispute. I'm saying this is information for the president. I'm not challenging any of this. When we prepare an integral report for the president, it consists of a string of summaries for different areas, from Banja Luka, Bijeljina, Doboj, Sarajevo, Herzegovina, Trebinje, and the analytical service that receives 20 to 30 dispatches from the ground would prepare a brief like this. We do not create briefs. I don't write them. I gather them. They send them to me and then I shape them into this sort of report for the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6538, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm aware of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will have a break for half an hour and resume at 3 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Back to your statement, paragraph 53, you say that you know -- you knew that there were prisoners of war after the fall of Srebrenica, and you were keeping the president informed; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. The president and the minister of the interior. The figures that were stated in our documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You had operatives in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. I had an operative who went from Zvornik to Bratunac every day and returned every afternoon. He wasn't based there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Radovic, your subordinate, was in Bratunac when Mustafic was released, wasn't he, on the 12th/13th July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Radovic's chief of centre led this operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Right. So he's in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, he directed the operation concerning Mr. Ibran Mustafic and his transfer to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We know now, don't we, that at the very least, the very least, you received that ICRC report we saw you forwarded to the president, that ICRC report dealing with events in Srebrenica between 10th and 16th July, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly which report you are referring to, but if it's the one that was mentioned a moment ago, we did not have any reporting from the ICRC on the 10th and 11th of July. I don't remember that you showed me that it was continual reporting. It was one report, as far as I was able to see, from your ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not going to go back to the document previously. We saw the report that you forwarded to the president, the ICRC report. We saw what it supposedly related to. You described it as relating to the period between 10 and 16 July. I'm quoting your letter to the president; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. If that's what's written in the document, then that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You knew there were thousands of prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say thousands. Our documents do not refer to thousands. We were referring to prisoners of war, but not in the thousands. If you look at our reports from the 10th and the 11th, I don't think the figure reaches even 1.000. 300 up to 500 are mentioned in our reports. If you take all our reports together, you will see that if you sum up all the figures, it's somewhere up to 500 prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We're not looking at 10th and 11th, you are clear about that, aren't you; right? It's after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: The period after, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: All right, so what you say is that you knew about up to 500 prisoners, 500 prisoners. That's all you knew about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that now, but knowing how the reporting went, I believe figures like 200, 300, were mentioned, up to 5 00. The figure of up to 500 is circulating through our reports. Of course, I'm not talking about the people who were transferred to Tuzla. I don't think you mean them. There is eight and a half thousand that left in the first wave and later up to the 23.000 who were taken in at the Tuzla airport by the Nordic Battalion. I don't think you mean these people. They were not prisoners of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So this is your evidence. Everyone else knows about thousands of prisoners and you, head of the DB, up to 500; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's how it turns out. I have to tell you again that POWs were not in the jurisdiction of the State Security Service, those were military captives, we had no access to military units, nor did we have that many men in that area of Srebrenica. We had one man, I emphasise one man, and he was accompanied by one young man, they formed the same team and we were not able to cover such a large area because people were taken prisoner --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] You know at the end of the war, don't you, end of 1995, you know that there are only less than 200 prisoners from Srebrenica at Batkovic. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I've read that somewhere. We were not monitoring Batkovic, so I don't know how many prisoners were there, Batkovic was also not in the jurisdiction of the State Security Service, but I've read somewhere that there was, I don't know how large a number of prisoners in Batkovic, who were later exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You've got a list of prisoners from Batkovic from the VRS, your subordinate Goran Radovic sent a communication to the VRS intelligence and security organs, for the East Bosnia Corps, identifying from that list persons of interest. You knew there were prisoners from Srebrenica in Batkovic; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That number that you mentioned, we knew that prisoners were in Batkovic and the military security service asked us if we had any information about persons from the area of Srebrenica. And, as far as I know, our service produced a document concerning the people we knew something about but that's four or five people. Some people we knew were somehow involved in the military operations in and around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Knowing, as you did, the large number of prisoners captured, detained, after the fall of Srebrenica, knowing as you did that less than a couple of hundred made it to Batkovic, did you not wonder what had happened to the others?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I am trying to explain to you that we were not monitoring where the -- the army was placing its prisoners of war. We had nothing to do with POWs. That letter by Mr. Radovic is a response to a request from the military security service asking us to give them some information about certain people who were at that time in prison but we did not know how many were in prison at the time. I don't know if you understand. That letter by Mr. Radovic was a response to the request made by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Isn't it right, Mr. Kijac, that you didn't wonder where the POWs were because you knew, didn't you? You knew that they were bound, blindfolded and buried in pits; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: You are again imputing to me something that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: David Rohde, you talk about him in your statement, he's a journalist who wrote for a publication called the "Christian Science Monitor." He wrote an article about the executions -- about executions following the fall of Srebrenica in August 1995. You're now aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I don't know that he wrote a news story. I know about David Rohde but I don't know about his article.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well you know about him because you arrested him in Zvornik municipality. He was arrested by the DB, wasn't he, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: It's not the State Security Service that arrested him. He was arrested by members of the public security station because he did not have the proper papers for entering to Republika Srpska and no documents allowing him to stay there. They arrested him because he was of security interest, and if you go back to that report from 1992, you will see that journalists and reporters were of security interest and were monitored as far as we were able to monitor them. It was the public security that arrested David Rohde and since he was of security interest, the matter was transferred to the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have P05227, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's the DB, wasn't it, who initiated proceedings against David Rohde; right? The charge -- you charged him, the DB charged him, and then he was prosecuted, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes, we filed a criminal complaint on the grounds of illegal entry into Republika Srpska, lack of proper documents, and that was not the first time. There had been journalists earlier against whom we had taken measures because they were not in possession of valid documents to enter Republika Srpska. They had certain documents that enabled foreign journalists to be in Republika Srpska, but David Rohde did not have such papers at the moment when he was arrested by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Come on, Mr. Kijac. We know he wasn't -- he wasn't in reality charged and prosecuted because he didn't have proper documents, was he? The real crime, the real crime, of David Rohde, his real crime, was that he was finding and he was photographing the execution sites, wasn't he, at Petkovci dam and Orahovac; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I think that everything is written in this document you have shown me, so it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So he's arrested on the 29th of October, first paragraph, yes? Second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- you report he's got military maps on which places where crimes against the Muslims had been committed were clearly marked, yes? He stated that he was visiting the general localities of Krizevici, that's the execution site at Orahovac, isn't it, and Djulici in Zvornik. That's what he's actually saying. You find -- you talked to him, he's photographing, he's got maps, that's what you're reporting here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to comment on this first sentence and then the rest. The first sentence says that due to unlawful presence and photographing in the area of Zvornik, he was arrested and all the later that you quote is the statement of David Rohde given to the state security organs, so there is no paraphrasing here other than the paraphrasing of the statements made by David Rohde to the state security operatives who interviewed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Look, we know what crimes he was prosecuted for. We know the misdemeanours with which he was charged under RS law. We have in evidence P06424, the request to initiate criminal proceedings, and at P06423, the detention order, signed by your Goran Radovic, your subordinate. We have got all this. We've seen all this. I want to ask you about what you've written here in this report, okay? So he says that he discovered the precise location of a place marked on the map in the Krizevici area, that's Orahovac; right? He's found evidence of crimes at the sites. He's found an ID card, military ID. He's photographed the items that he found. You seize all this documentation from him; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Reference is made here to what he said. He said that on the instructions of some people he came to the area of Srebrenica and headed for certain locations, so he was in Krizevici and found, in his own words, evidence, namely, one ID and one military service book belonging to people of Muslim nationality. If one ID and one military service book are evidence of crimes, then I have no further comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: 65 ter 25255, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In the spirit of co-operation, this is supposedly at a time when military relations, military-civilian relations were not good, according to you in your statement, the VRS Main Staff security, Beara, he writes to you about Rohde, tells you, doesn't he, that people are looking for him, internationals, yes? Have I accurately summarised the content of this communication? Yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that I didn't sign this dispatch. I see it for the first time. It was signed obviously by my deputy, and I am seeing it for the first time, but there is nothing in this letter that is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I seek to tender that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we looking at the same letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Main Staff, administration for security, 3rd November, 1995, signed by Chief Colonel Ljubisa Beara. You see there is no signature here in longhand. It must be the signature of my deputy because at that time we were in the area of Krajina. I see this letter for the first time. I suppose my people acted upon this dispatch and he was prosecuted before a court of law.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This followed, this followed, didn't it, your communication, your communication, to the VRS security administration that we just previously saw; right? This is referring to your communication. You see that? It's got a number there at the top, 053368-95; right? Don't disagree with that, do you? No?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I am not questioning that the previous letter was from the state security department at the security administration of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is a response to that; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No. This is not a response. It's their request.
