We had informed them that we had taken certain measures against Mr. Rohde, and perhaps Mr. Ljubisa Beara had not received our information because our information was addressed to the intelligence administration, that is to say Colonel Salapura; whereas Colonel Ljubisa Beara, as far as I know, was head of the military security, that is to say military police, and we had very little co-operation with them. We had very -- we had most of the co-operation with the intelligence of administration of the VRS headed by Colonel Salapura; whereas with Ljubisa Beara, who was chief of the military police, we had very little co-operation. And it's possible that Ljubisa Beara had not received the letter we had sent previously. And then on the same day he asked for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Do we have to spend a lot of time on this? This document refers to your previous telegram, okay; right? You'd agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Apparently so. But I'm trying to explain to you that we had no correspondence with the military police and the military security. We had correspondence with the intelligence administration branch of the military security, not with the military security proper headed by Colonel Beara. It's possible that Colonel Beara had no access to the previous document except that he somehow got hold of it. It's obvious that this is sent to us from the military security, it's sent to the state security, that's all evident. It's evident that my deputy signed it and it's dated 3rd November, 1995, and nothing in the document is in issue. This is the first time I see it. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] to have admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6539, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question for Mr. Kijac. To be clear, do you say that Mr. Beara had access to your telegram which was sent to this intelligence or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, obviously, yes, because you can see that the link is to our telegram. However, our telegrams were never sent to Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the answer is yes, that's fine. Let's continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just one last matter on Rohde, P06424.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just very quickly so we are clear about the crimes, the misdemeanours under RS law for which he was charged, for which he was prosecuted, the first charge we've dealt with, this is the request to initiate criminal proceedings from Goran Radovic, RDB centre chief Bijeljina, your subordinate. The first charge relates to the falsification of personal documents which you've spoken about. The second charge on page 2 of the English, please, still on page 1 of the B/C/S, is that he goes to the red mud dam in the area of the village Petkovci. That's the Petkovci dam, and he takes photographs. That's the second misdemeanour with which he is charged; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We can see the evidence is identified at the following page in B/C/S, same page in English, you can see the evidence against him includes the photographs that he took at the time, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your interest here, you personally, in the DB, your interest after the Srebrenica events, let me just go back a moment. This was the one and only prosecution, wasn't it, prosecution initiated by the MUP after the Srebrenica events; right? This is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I don't know how you mean that, the only one. I mean, if you mean in terms of crime, there were probably more criminal reports. We, as a service, hardly ever file criminal reports. Very seldom. We are an information service. And only in certain situations that have to do with the foreign factor we are the ones who possibly file criminal reports. This is not the only one of the State Security Service in that period, but I assume that the Ministry of the Interior had many more criminal reports and that period. I don't really know what you mean. Please try to explain to me what it is that you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: What I mean is that in 1995, the only person who was arrested and prosecuted for matters related to Srebrenica events, right, following the Srebrenica events, was a journalist who was trying to find out the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the State Security Service is concerned, that was the only case; that is to say, we worked with him because this has to do with foreign national and conditions were right to file a report because he was illegally staying in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You in the DB, your interest, was only ever in repressing the investigation of the mass executions, wasn't it? This is what you did. You covered up Srebrenica crimes; right? You personally.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Again, you're imputing something which is wrong. I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No comment because you're unsure of the answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, I think I've answered. I didn't want to take it any further. That's why I said that I had no further comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me remind you of what's going on in October/November 1995, when this man was prosecuted for taking photographs of Petkovci dam. Just remind you. In September/October, executed Muslim men were reburied. They were shovelled from pits in Bratunac and Zvornik to other pits in Bratunac and Zvornik. Roads were sealed off. This was a significant logistical effort. Civilian and military assets were deployed; right? You were aware of the reburials, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. The first time I came across this was in Mr. Butler's report, I think in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: One person who was interviewed by the OTP described the environment of Bratunac when the bodies were being shifted from pit to pit. I'll read it as follows, 65 ter 25722, if anyone wants to follow, but it's in English so I'll just read it. He says: "There were lorries transporting bodies for hours, even children along the side of the road were finding arms and legs." Later he says: "I didn't see it but I could smell it. I could smell the stench." A bit later he says: "I know what the sketch was when I smelled it because it's very characteristic, the smell of a human body which is decomposing." Now, you had operatives in the area --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we see it in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's pages 76, please in the English. There is no B/C/S, I'm afraid. That's all I'm going to read. Just want to ask the witness a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You'd operatives in the area, in Bratunac and Zvornik. Putrefying human bodies were being shifted from pit to pit, and you're seriously telling us here today that you weren't aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, you did talk to my operatives, I will accept everything that they said to you. If they said that they knew about the transfer of bodies, I will accept that because I cannot deny it then. However, in the statements of persons that you talked to from the Zvornik department, there is no mention of transfers and there is no mention of relocating these graves, on the one hand. On the other hand, you know that sometime around the 11th, in one of our reports, there is mention - I think it's the 11th or 12th of July - that in Srebrenica, there are corpses of animals and people, and you have in this report that 40 of our people, members of the police, were infected because the terrain had not been sanitised. So what is being said is maybe true but I did not receive a single paper stating what you said just now, especially, as far as I know, not a single one of our operatives gave that kind of information to you. If you have information provided by my operatives, then I will say that that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that report about Srebrenica town, about animals, I'm talking about -- just help me with this: How is it possible, please, Mr. Kijac, how is it possible that you were not aware thousands of men had gone missing, thousands of them, and then their bodies were shoveled from pit to pit for everyone to see and to smell and you are seriously, seriously, saying to this Court that you knew nothing about this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I mean, on the 25th of July, an offensive was launched against the Krajina, that is to say the Grahovo and Glamoc theatre of war an offensive started, and before the 1st of August I was in the area of Krajina and I stayed there for almost two months. At that time, our positions were also being bombed so the operatives already then, you're talking about September and October, they were collecting completely different information, intelligence, in terms of where the enemy is going to launch offensives, what the targets of the bombing aircraft are going to be, nobody thought about this. You have to look at the time and conditions under which all of this was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Nobody was --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it was marked, but in line 11, it doesn't say I stayed there for about two months in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your president is indicted with Mladic, wasn't he, in November 1995, for genocide arising out of the Srebrenica events. You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: On the 16th of January, 1996, you, by now minister, the highest, most senior law enforcement official in the Republika Srpska, you order the public security department in Bijeljina to provide fake IDs for eight members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Could I take a look at that paper?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Do you agree or do you not agree with my question? I've asked you a question, can you answer it yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Could I please take a look at that paper?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: P04491, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is a document from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you say, Mr. Kijac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know this paper by heart but I asked to have a look at this so that I could explain to the Prosecutor that this paper was sent to me by the intelligence administration of the Main Staff. So the intelligence administration is asking for eight passports or identity papers - it doesn't matter - for their people. Since this was a normal type of communication between the Main Staff and the organs of the Ministry of the Interior, I forwarded that to the Ministry of the Interior to the head of public security, instructing them to have passports provided to them, because, as I've already said, there was always this co-operation between military and state security, when their people needed to travel abroad, then, as a rule, under quotation marks, false identity papers are issued to them. So these papers are issued on the basis of requests put forth by them and then there is documentation to that effect. At the request of the Main Staff eight passports were issued, we don't know who these persons were, and possibly if some day a problem occurs, then people can see which organ asked the ministry for these papers. Your Honours, that was standing practice since time immemorial, if I can put it that way, between the Ministry of the Interior and the military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: There was co-operation, wasn't there, between the military and state security when it came to covering up Srebrenica crimes; isn't that right? That's when you co-operated. That's what this is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: There was excellent co-operation between military security and military intelligence and the state securities service but not along the lines along which you want me to give an answer. We exchanged information on a daily basis that was of security interest. I know what you're getting at, Srebrenica. But I'm telling you once again: From all of our documents, you can see what was sent to the military and what the military sent to us. Unfortunately, I cannot give a positive answer to your question except for the part, what I already said, that we had good co-operation, that is my estimate in terms of this exchange of security information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Help me with this. This document is talking about a group of members in the 10th Sabotage Detachment who are supposedly on a list of individuals who have been indicted by The Hague Tribunal; right? It's talking about Erdemovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Ademovic"] and seven others who were involved in executing Muslim prisoners at Branjevo farm, right, and you knew that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: To this day, to this day, I don't know who these passports were made for. That was not standing practice. It would not be a secret if the minister of the interior knew who these passports were being issued to, and these papers were being issued to persons so that they could travel abroad mainly; that is to say, so that they could safely stay outside the territory of Republika Srpska so they could carry out certain assignments, so they would not travel with their own passports. So I absolutely do not know about the organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska because I left the army in 1980, as an ordinary soldier. So how do I put this? I do not really know about military structure. I did not even know about their 10th Sabotage Detachment. I knew the Main Staff and the corps commanders, and in that segment I knew the organs, the securities or intelligence organs, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you agree, Mr. Kijac, that this document itself refers to ten individuals that have been indicted by The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, to this day, I don't know whether these persons were accused by The Hague Tribunal. I think that Mr. Salapura worded this a bit columnsily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whether this document states so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what is written in the document, Your Honour. But to this day, I -- I do not know the names of these persons to this day. Now, Ms. Pack mentioned some names and I really don't know about these names, and I don't know any of these people personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were protecting them, you were shielding them from arrest, weren't you? That's what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I don't understand how you mean that, shielding them. Could you please be so kind as to clarify that for me? We were protecting certain persons, yes, that was the department for the protection of certain officials, and that is what that part of the service did, whereas these persons were not protected by the service. How could I protect persons whose names I do not know?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: On April -- in April 1996, Karadzic issued an order to you and other organs of state to investigate the Srebrenica events, P00164. Don't need to look at it, but that's the reference. Now, at this time, Erdemovic, one of the shooters at Branjevo farm, had been transferred to The Hague, hadn't he? You must have been aware of that. He was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we have the name again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My apologies. The name of the document is P000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no. The name of the shooter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Erdemovic, Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Erdemovic. It's noted as "Ademovic."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's probably my tone and my pronunciation. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: He, Erdemovic, 10th Sabotage Detachment, Branjevo farm, he had been indicted. He had been transferred to The Hague 30th of March, 1996. You were aware of that. You were head of the MUP, the minister.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I learned that from the media. That was not done by the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Of course you knew about it at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You knew he was -- in the international media? You were following the international media then, were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No. No. The Serb media.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: He was indicted, you know that, in May for his participation in the executions at Branjevo military farm? You know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No. Individually, I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You knew minister --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, it wasn't individually, it was details. He said that he did not know the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Kijac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got, I think, five or six minutes left. And it may be that I'll be five or six minutes longer if I deal with two more documents which I'd ask if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Chamber has no difficulty with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You know minister of the interior that ICTY investigators are on the ground in the RS in 1996 exhuming bodies and carrying out forensic investigations; right? You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: To a very small extent in 1996, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have P04308.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I just want to look at some of the investigative work that was being carried out in 1996 by foreign investigators in your territory in the RS. So page 141 of e-court, please. This is very briefly. Forensic investigations being carried out in April. You can see the date stamp there, April 1996, evidence in the case supports that this is the date on which this photo was taken. So there we are. And this is at Orahovac. That's the evidence in this case. Orahovac, you remember, from your arrest of David Rohde in October 1995; right? I'll just show you another -- another photograph demonstrating the investigations being carried out by ICTY investigators. There were at Petkovci. Just show you briefly at page 180 in e-court. It's the dam. Remember we spoke about that earlier. Date stamped April 1996. We move to 187, at Petkovci, and it's 7 of e-court, digging up bones. If we go to Pilica, page 242 of e-court, please. Are you looking at the pictures? You can see these investigations taking place in 1996. You agree all these investigations are taking place, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Probably. This is the first time I see these photographs, even the locations don't say a thing to me. I mean whether it's here or there, I don't -- actually, I was not in the area of Srebrenica. So to be quite frank, I don't know the area, so the names of these villages and hamlets don't say a thing to me. This is the first time I see these photographs and I can say that in that year, 1996, when these excavations started, the belief was that this was sanitisation of the terrain and that these were persons who were killed in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Looking here at this picture here at page 242, August 1996 is the date on that, the preceding page you can see that because there is an investigator and a time stamp in Pilica dom, and that's just the wall, the blood spattered wall at Pilica dom. Following page, 244, please. These were the investigations that were being carried out in 1996 by ICTY investigators. And then Branjevo Farm, page 255, please. This is a photograph which is taken during the exhumation which took place between the 10th and the 24th of September at Branjevo Farm. This is a photo taken during the exhumation. It's a disturbed mass grave. You can see that, can't you? There is a big pit but only about 100 bodies there where those three people are standing. You can see that photograph, can't you, what it depicts, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I see that. I see these three men.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And the following page, these are the bodies that remain in the grave, the grave at Branjevo Farm; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I don't know where they are from. These are corpses, you're right. I don't know at all what you're getting at. I'm not familiar with these locations. When you say Branjevo to me, it's as if you told me the name of a street here in The Hague. I was never in the area. So I mean, I don't even know where Branjevo is, where Pilica is. I mean I know by the names that that is the area of the municipality of Srebrenica, but I was never there and I cannot say anything except for these pictures. I see the pictures now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You are the head of the Ministry of the Interior. These are investigations which were being conducted by the ICTY in the RS in 1996. You are ordered by the president, ordered by the president, apparently, to investigate Srebrenica. And you produce, let's look at it, a report in September 1996, P00165. Let's look at your report. Recognise it, your report? This is the MUP's investigation into Srebrenica. If we can go over, I think, in the B/C/S the following two pages. It's a two-page report. One paragraph devoted to the actual killings. One paragraph. Look at your conclusions. Just look at the first paragraph. You say that the Muslims killed each other as a chain reaction. There were suicides. All of them? That was the outcome of your investigations, thousands of men killed themselves, killed each other, chain reaction? That was the outcome of the investigation, an investigation undertaken by the minister of interior into the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I don't know what investigation you are talking about. This is a report to either the assistant or the deputy minister of justice. This is not an investigation. This is a report of the RDB which obtained this information having conducted an interview with a person, one individual, and then under a cover letter I sent it to the Ministry of Justice, which at that time had started some talks with representatives of the international community, i.e., representatives of the ICTY. This is not -- this doesn't refer to any investigation. If you look at the heading, you will see who it is addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's your evidence, is it, there was no investigation by the MUP, no investigation by the MUP following the Srebrenica events, following the Srebrenica events of crimes against the Muslim men who were executed? No investigation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I did not have any information indicating that an investigation was being conducted. I stress that as the chief of the department, I had no information that I had -- I had no information about the executions and when I assumed the position of minister, I received no information to the effect that something of the kind had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So when the president issued an order in April 1996 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, can we see that again?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: P00164, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kijac, do you agree that Mr. Karadzic ordered you to investigate the Srebrenica event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly speaking, I do not remember this paper. Maybe I might have seen it in 2002 or 2003. I can see that there are a number of addressees here and a number of institutions, and that is all that I can say here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree you received this from Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall that, but Your Honours, we did not conduct any investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You didn't conduct an investigation, you wrote this report from your desk in Pale, because no one ever intended that those events be investigated, did they? All you could do is write a one-paragraph -- one paragraph in your cover-up report because everyone knew, everyone knew, didn't they, about the killings, as they were taking place; right? That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: You can say that if that were a report about investigation in Srebrenica it would be addressed to President Karadzic rather than to the assistant minister of justice, and it would say pursuant to your order, so and so, the ministry has acted, so on and so on, has obtained this information. It would not be addressed to a person of a much lower ranking person than I myself was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You didn't bother investigating Srebrenica events after this order was issued by Dr. Karadzic because you knew it wasn't a serious order, didn't you? It wasn't seriously intended that you investigate events about which you all knew, was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I have to repeat, I stick to my previous answer. I have already answered that question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Karadzic re-examines you, I have some questions. When asked by Ms. Pack -- when asked by Ms. Pack whether up to 500 was all that you knew, you said while agreeing with that but you said -- also said, "I cannot" -- I quote, "I cannot say that now." Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I remember having said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As you sit there now, what do you know as to the number of prisoners, the number of victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what I read in Butler's 2002 report, that is approximately all that I know about Srebrenica. I got hold of it in 2003 or 2004. Somebody gave it to me. I read a report. In the meanwhile, I also perused some other documents and examined them but that is a different thing altogether. But this knowledge that I have is post [indiscernible] thing as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When did you first read Butler's report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know it was drawn up in 2002, so after that year, after 2002. That is one of the versions which I had occasion to see, possibly it was supplemented subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Had you read Mr. Butler's report at that time, then I wonder how you could say when Ms. Pack said Branjevo to you, you said it sounded as if she told the name of a street here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, Your Honours, I'm not familiar with that terrain. I'm not talking about hindsight, about things I learned subsequently. I was talking about what I knew in 1995, not about what I learned after 2005. So when I'm offered this to see, I have to relate to what I know about that particular period and not 2005 or 2010 or 2015, or perhaps we did not exactly understand each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency just a couple of questions. Can we have this document, P001064 on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kijac, can you tell us, in principle, when are documents -- when documents of this kind are sent, where do you actually indicate who is in charge of executing a specific assignment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Well, you have put it here, in certain order, as it were. The protagonists, the factors who are to participate in the collection of information for investigation, so if you'll allow me to say this is more than anything a job for the prosecutions, for the prosecutor's office and then the prosecutor's office enjoins upon other organs to undertake certain measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with what His Excellency the president asked you, can you tell us whether you had the impression, without asking you for the precise figure, how many prisoners did we have from the beginning to the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No. There is a document that I got hold of in 1996, someone writing to us in connection with POWs, and we responded that we had no exact data, that we only knew that there were very many POWs in Krajina, in Herzegovina, in Sarajevo, et cetera. So I cannot talk about the actual figures because I really don't know them, only those within whose jurisdiction POWs were can talk about the figures, primarily military organs. I did come across some documents preparing myself for this. I found some lists, but never generally as a State Security Service, I have to reiterate, we never dealt with POWs because that was strictly within the ambit of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you -- as a State Security Service, during the war, did you come by any information to the effect that there had been executions of some of these many thousands of POWs that we had in the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: No. And I believe that I've already stated that, that we didn't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 56, you were asked in connection with the request of the Main Staff, can you tell us when did Republika Srpska adopt a law on obligatory co-operation with The Hague and was it in existence at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I could not give you an answer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Document -- in that document, where Beara responds to you, he says in the first sentence, we found about your telegram from our source, can you tell us how you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I don't understand it in any specific way. If he indicates the reference to our dispatch, that means he has read our paper, and on the basis of our paper, he's communicating with us. He actually refers to our paper, while stating that he receives this information from the source. Obviously there was no communication within them, within the VRS security services when it comes to that particular paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It follows that David Rohde was observed near the dam. Can you tell us whether the dams on a river or at the dumb sites were of any security related interest for Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Not for Republika Srpska. That was also the case in the former Yugoslavia. No one could photograph any dam or near it at any specific distance. There were signs actually prohibiting access to any such facility which was of security interest for the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have information that there was a danger or any plans for some dams along the Drina River to be demolished by the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some -- there was some information about sabotage groups being infiltrated into specific areas, certain areas, and we sent that information to security organs in the field where we thought, where we assessed such terrorist groups could actually undertake such actions at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can witness be shown 1D5555.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is no translation, so please present this document to the Chamber. Can you tell us what the heading is, what unit is, what's the date? You don't have to read it out aloud, just look at it. Look at what Oric is proposing or requesting actually.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: This is a request for a precise locations to be given, specified, of the hydro power plant in Bajina Basta so that the sabotage groups of Naser Oric could blow it up and prepare themselves for demolishing it. They need a plan, a man who is familiar with it, and the particular spot where to plant the explosives. So they are looking for an expert to specify the spots at which the explosives should be laid and also a guide to lead them for safe conduct of the group to the dam at Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 19th of December, 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the 19th of December, 1994, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber what the consequences downstream from that dam would have been had they managed to actually blow up the dam?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: They would have been disastrous, formidable, any breaking of the dam or demolition of the dam would of course entail huge consequences in the area which would be flooded by the waters and of course the population would suffer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: That would mean both Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would red mud dam demolition -- what consequences would it entail, what is this red mud, if you know, the red sludge, and what would the consequences be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know this facility, believe me. As I've already said, I have never been to the area but the consequence would have been terrible because, generally speaking, if you demolish any dam and the waters that are released of course, destroy everything on their path.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just wondering the point of this question. Is it your case, Mr. Karadzic, that Mr. Rohde was arrested to protect this dam?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, what I'm saying is that he was observed for the first time near the dam, and he was observed because the people were watching, people and citizens were watching the dam because it was dangerous for anyone to get near the dam. And dams -- that is why he was observed there. And the dams were a major concern of ours at that time, of course. And incidentally, this also speaks about the danger from the 28th Division, i.e. the 8th Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives MFI number D4160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, you stated that not only Rohde but -- and not only in 1995 but throughout the war, we had had reason to inquire or to be interested in the conduct, in the behaviour, of foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we see 1D9512? Can we bring that up in e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we have no translation of that either so I would ask you to introduce this document to the Chamber too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check the number? And whether it has been published?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have it. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who is sending this to whom and who is this gentleman, Mr. Ceranic, who is sending the document to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Mr. Ceranic was the chief of the State Security Service for the area of Sarajevo. He is informing us hereby that the journalists of the British agency Sky News are using forged certificates with the signature of the president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic, enabling them to work unhindered in the territory of Republika Srpska. And, generally speaking, you can see in every work programme, that the State Security Service was monitoring journalists as security interesting persons because of the connections, contacts and information they had. That's how we found out occasionally about forged IDs and we got that information from our sources in journalist circles.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives MFI D4161, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked how come you never wondered what became of those people, those combatants, and you gave your answers, but now I would like to show you 1D9513, dated 22nd July, 1995. In this document, I see some information -- no, it's not the right document. 1D9513. You checked out some information and marked other information as unverified. Why are these designations important?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: I can't see the document yet. I don't have to read the document, if that's your only question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's one question and then I would like to ask you about paragraph 3 from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: So let me take up this one first. When we get information from the ground, they indicate the source and the level of verification. The information can be verified, reliable, or not. It can be in the process of verification, and it may be a product of operative techniques or it can be information emanating from a source we have been co-operating with for a long time, and know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read the third paragraph from the bottom? Can you read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: "According to reliable information, the RDB managed to extract from the area of Srebrenica about 7.000 members of the so-called BH army, 3500 of which would be engaged in the Sarajevo theatre of war. The government of the so-called BH is planning to place refugees from Zepa in Kladanj, and those from Gorazde in Zenica and Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that what you knew on the 22nd of July about the number of soldiers, men, who got out of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Yes. Through these papers, we have been following, we registered that 22.000 men got out and reached the Tuzla airport where they were taken in by the Nordic Battalion, and we had information that 7.000 combatants managed to get out in this breakthrough when the corridor was opened for them, I believe on the 16th. And I have to emphasise that that morning there was a skirmish between the VRS and those 7.000 men and in that skirmish, within two hours, we had 22 dead and -- 12 dead and more than 20 wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and take up his last sentence again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kijac, you are speaking too fast. Could you repeat from your -- from where -- where you said the "12 dead and more than 20 wounded"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So that morning there was a skirmish between the army and that group of men, those 7.000 members of the BH Army, who were getting out of Srebrenica. And we had 12 dead, I believe, and 82 wounded, although we were on top of a hill, set in an ambush with mortars and Pragas, et cetera. Then we had information that out of 500 men from that group, some managed to get out to Zepa, some military conscripts went to Gorazde. We had that information and we had information that more than a thousand men had crossed over into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Plus we had information that about 87 wounded from Bratunac had been transferred to the area of Tuzla. And you can see all that from the correspondence at the level of the State Security Service, at the headquarters, and the branch in Bijeljina, through reports from the 10th, let's say, until the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read out loud the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: "Through contacts with the Muslim Commission for Exchanges, their representatives asked for an exchange all for all, clearly aware of the fact that there are incomparably more Muslim soldiers captured by the VRS. They also insisted that there should be a contact between the two chairmans of the commissions for exchange and the so-called BH."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is your information about the status of POWs on the 22nd of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Already on the 12th, 13th and 14th, there was talk about an all-for-all exchange and Mr. Renovica, who at that time was chief of the department, says in one of his statements to investigators, he says that our attention is declining because there is already talk about an all-for-all exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are very often overlapping and do not leave any pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I just wanted to get in before the question was asked just to say that I didn't ask any questions about this topic, about exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So any further questions I just wanted to stop because, in my submission, it goes beyond the remit of my cross. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Pack. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can respond. The focus of this is not the exchange. The focus is on the awareness of this witness that there is a great number of prisoners, and the Prosecution was insisting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You took the issue of exchange from this document. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Ms. Pack. Please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why is this topic discussed at the end whereas the first paragraphs are about the events in Krajina? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC
utterances.text: Of course I can. At that time, the offensive of the Croatian army against Grahovo and Glamoc had already begun and we have intelligence that the Croatian army is concentrating in certain areas, and that the Croatian armed forces in co-ordinated action with the Muslim 5th Corps and the HVO would be attacking the western parts of Krajina. And as far as I know, a few days after this, I left for Krajina and you arrived there on the 1st of August and we both stayed there with a few breaks until the end of October, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives MFI D4162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we going to take -- shall we take a break or you would like to continue now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for Mr. Kijac and I only thank him for coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Kijac, for your testimony. Please have a safe journey back home. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we rise for lunch break, there are a couple of matters I'd like to deal with now. First, we will issue our oral ruling on Vidoje Blagojevic's request for the assignment of counsel for the purposes of his testimony in this case filed on the record on the 20th of November, 2013. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution indicated via e-mail on 21st November that it did not wish to respond to this request. The Chamber has considered Article 5 of the directive on the assignment of counsel, which provides for the assignment of counsel to three categories of individuals: Suspects, accused persons, and any persons detained under the authority of the Tribunal. Blagojevic was granted early release effective 31st of December, 2012, and is therefore no longer covered by Article 5 of the directive. The Chamber sees no exceptional circumstances warranting that the Chamber order the Registrar to assign counsel to Blagojevic for the purpose of his testimony in these proceedings, and the request is therefore denied. Next I have a question for Mr. Karadzic. On the 29th of November, 2013, the accused filed his Defence submission of order of witnesses for January and February 2014 with a confidential annex appending the names of 65 witnesses. This list does not include your name, Mr. Karadzic. According to the Chamber's internal calculations, it is expected that you should call your last witness around the end of February. The Chamber was under the impression, given the various representations you have made, that you would be the last witness to testify in your case and that you wished to apportion a significant amount of your time to that effect. Is that still the case, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I could answer that because I was the one who prepared the filing. Our calculations are that our case will finish sometime in March, the beginning or middle of March, so that's why we didn't include all of our witnesses on that list. This is the projection of witnesses for January and February. So I think the question of Dr. Karadzic testifying is still under consideration but we are still reserving 16 hours for his testimony and it's anticipated that he would be the last witness, but the reason he's not on that list is because we believe that we will go through January and February and not run out of our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please bear in mind that the Chamber will not grant the Defence additional time for that purpose so that the Defence should organise itself according to the 325 hours in total that has been granted. We will resume at 25 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. Please make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Tadic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled under such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you, for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: May God be with you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting, I mean, for the interpretation. So I'm asking you also to pause and enunciate your sentences slowly so that it could all be reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D9528 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement of yours before you on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read the statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness please be shown the last page so that he could identify his signature. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you communicated to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: They would be the same or similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection. However, we would note that many of the statements, or rather, many of the questions in this statement are formulated in an extremely leading fashion; for instance, questions 21, 22 and 27 contain multiple obviously leading questions and also others questions invite the witness to draw conclusions on legal issues. And so, in the Prosecution's submission, these would go to the weight of the evidence in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will admit the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit D4163, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out in the English language a brief summary of Mr. Boro Tadic's statement. [In English] Boro Tadic was the commander of the 1st Battalion of the 6th Sana Infantry Brigade of the JNA and the chief of the Secretariat of National Defence. In the spring of 1992, the situation in BH was getting worse. In light of this, in April 1992, the JNA's 6th Krajina Brigade returned to Sanski Most with the task of preserving peace and preventing interethnic conflicts. The brigade controlled the area and provided protection to everyone, regardless of their ethnicity. However, fighting broke out and there were open attacks on the army by the Muslim paramilitary forces. The Muslim paramilitary forces refused to surrender their illegal weapons and attacked the army and the police. Boro Tadic was directly involved in negotiations with Muslims and Croats regarding the preservation of peace and resolution of conflict in a peaceful way. However, Muslim extremists refused to co-operate. Living conditions in the area in general were very harsh for all ethnic groups. Everyone, regardless of religion or ethnicity, suffered equally. Boro Tadic recalls that President Karadzic ordered that he and his colleagues respect international conventions and protect all citizens regardless of their nationality. The obligation to respect the laws of war, especially the Geneva Conventions, and Additional Protocols were stressed. Steps were taken to conduct investigations into crimes against Muslims and Croats committed by the members of Serb community. Mr. Boro Tadic's unit in Sanski Most did not engage volunteers and no one supported the paramilitaries. In March 1992, Muslims created barricades to control everyone passing through their villages. They killed a Serb at one of the barricades in the village of Trnovo. Boro Tadic believes that between April 1990 and April 1992, the leaders of the SDA and the HDZ had planned to destroy the SFRY. The Serbs tried to find a solution for all ethnic groups to live together in a common state. However, because of the actions of the SDA and HDZ leadership, the Serbs were forced to establish bodies to defend the people's interests. The Crisis Staffs were not used as a means to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims or Croats from BH. There were no policies of persecution, forced deportation or ethnic cleansing. Before the first multi-party elections, Mr. Boro Tadic was a member of parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina and was politically very active. And that is all for that moment. I do not have questions for Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Tadic, as you have noted, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is through your written statement. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, first I would very briefly like to clarify the various roles that you had. Before the war, from 1986 to 1990, you were a deputy in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly; is that correct? I'm afraid you have to answer --

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I was in the assembly. That was the last assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, before the multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. May I just at the outset ask you to listen to my questions carefully and answer them as concisely as possible, so that's a yes-no answer where possible, and also just to remind you that you will need to make a verbal response for the purposes of the record. So you were a founding member of the SDS in Sanski Most in August 1990; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And we've heard that you served in the JNA and you were appointed commander of the 1st Battalion of the 6th Brigade on the 3rd of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, you note in your statement that the 6th Brigade was deployed back from Western Slavonia to Sanski Most in early April 1992. In May 1992, you were a member of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I was assistant commander for moral and religious affairs when I returned from the hospital in Sarajevo, that was in April and May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But you were also a member of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Later, in the month of June, I was appointed head of department in the Ministry of Defence, which is an organ of Republika Srpska, and is in charge of mobilisation in the territory of municipality of Sanski Most. So I attended sessions of the Executive Board only as a guest, when questions from my line of work were discussed with a view to co-ordinating the activities related to mobilisation, in terms of the resource that is exist in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, could you come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P2614.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tadic, this is a document issued by the Crisis Staff of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly and you'll see at subparagraph 1(a) of the document, it states -- and, excuse me, the document is dated the 30th of May, 1992, and it states, the Crisis Staff consists of the following 12 persons. Each one having a clear domain of activities. And if you go down to number 5, you will see your name as secretary of the People's Defence Secretariat. So it's true, isn't it, Mr. Tadic, that you were, in fact, a member of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: At the time, war operations were underway and I was in Lusci Palanka, that's where I was born and that's where I lived. So when this conclusion was adopted, when the Crisis Staff was appointed, I didn't even know about that at that point in time. Later on, when the situation became such that I could come to work, that was sometime, say, mid-June, I only attended on behalf of -- actually, we called this the Executive Board, although it was the Crisis Staff. So this was a transition in order to have certain things that needed to be resolved properly. So this was a Crisis Staff in actual fact, but actually this was a temporary body that no longer existed later on because I was not appointed head of the Secretariat for National Defence because according to the constitution of Republika Srpska when there were no more secretariats when there was only the department of defence of Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, again I'd like you to keep your answers as concise as possible. But just to clarify, on the 15th of July, 1992, you were appointed head of the municipal department for National Defence; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I did not quite understand. Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: My question is: On the 15th of July, 1992, you were appointed the head of the municipal department for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Department, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back a little to your first relations or your earlier relations with Mr. Karadzic, you've known him since at least 1990; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the assembly of the republic, I spoke about the situation in Yugoslavia, and that is how we met, when the Serb Democratic Party was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And together with him, you arranged for a gathering of the SDS in September 1990 at Lusci Palanka, attended by him, Mr. Raskovic and various other leaders of the SDS; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, in response to your question number 38 you state that you had no knowledge that the SDS state bodies or Karadzic spread propaganda among the Bosnian Serbs and specifically you say in relation to the danger that Bosnian Serbs could be victims of genocide. And you also say, in your response to question number 21(f), that the Serbs tried to calm the situation and prevent conflict. Now, on the 3rd of March, 1991, there was an SDS rally in Banja Luka which was attended by Mr. Karadzic, Ms. Plavsic, Jovan Raskovic and various others. Do you recall this rally?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I was in hospital in Sarajevo at the time, from the 17th of March until the 2nd of April. I was at the military hospital in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Do you recall hearing of this rally?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It was in the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter number 40516A. And I'm interested in time code 1.44.11 to 1.45.04.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic I'd just like to play you a few excerpts from that rally, if my colleague could switch to Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The Yugoslav People's Army units entered Pakrac to count dead Serbs. Ustashas took away bound Serbs under their passive surveillance. Ustashas' nest has been made on the bell-tower of the Orthodox church in Pakrac. Nobody knows what happened to Father Savo Bosanac. It is said that he died trying to stop Ustashas from entering the church. This is exactly the proof that the same bestial spirituality and frantic despotism commits the same genocide as it did between" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there perhaps a transcript with a translation? Because what is reflected in the transcript is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We were not interpreting, we were reading from a transcript that was provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think there is a way you can check the transcript later on at any time with the assistance of Mr. Robinson or whoever.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in such situations, we are asked to provide a transcript, and I'm just asking whether that is also the duty of the other side as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can look at it immediately now with the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just wondering though -- I was a little bit surprised to hear that the interpreters were simply reading from the transcript. I thought that they would be making their best efforts to translate from what is being said with the aid of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That has been our practice, Mr. Robinson, with respect to these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I guess I was unaware of that. I always thought we were providing the transcript so that the interpreters could be assisted and they it would make their best interpretation from the evidence that's being heard. The transcripts are admitted so there is no reason to duplicate the same language in the transcript of our trial. I thought that they were actually interpreting what was being said but if that's not the case, that's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I found your submission surprising. It has been our practice given the difficulty of interpreting the language from the video or audio. Let us leave it at that. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So this speaker referring to the bestial spirituality and frantic despotism that commits the same genocide as it did between 1941 and 1945, you'll agree that contrary to your statement, this speaker was stating that the Bosnian Serbs were under threat of genocide in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: In our area, in Sanski Most, no one had to talk to us about that because in 1941, on the day of St. Elijah, five and a half thousand Serbs were killed in Susnjari and they had been tricked to coming to Sanski Most. And many, many, Serbs were taken to the Ustasha concentration camp of Jasenovac and killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic I'm going to interrupt you. Once again my question was: Did -- was this speaker referring to the threat of genocide in 1991? And I believe your answer is yes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the genocide that was committed by the Ustasha authorities against the Serbs, only in Jasenovac, 700.000 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to listen to what Mr. Karadzic said at that rally and that's at time code 2.14.34 to 2.15.50.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We are counting that today too we confirmed our authority that today too we received from you instructions on what to do. If we understood well, we have to do the following to fight for democracy because whenever there was democracy it was good for the Serb people: To fight for Yugoslavia; that is to say, for one state no matter how big it would be, where we would all live, to fight to accomplish political goals without violence. We will not start violence but if someone else starts it, we will have to accept it. And I can also tell you that Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly functions well only thanks to your delegates, but if it comes to the fall of authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you will still have your Serb National Council which will not let you be slaughtered like in 1941. Long live."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tadic, you'll agree that contrary to your statement, Karadzic's reference at this rally to Serbs being slaughtered in 1941 would not have calmed the situation but, rather, would have made Serbs more fearful.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: What I recall at that time was the truth taken from under the concrete, concrete, because thousands and thousands of Serbs were actually placed in pits over which concrete was poured in the communist era. So after so many years, the extractions of those bones of the holy martyrs of Serbs, of course, sowed fear among the nation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Once again, I didn't ask you for an account of the history of your region. I asked you whether Mr. Karadzic's statement would have calmed the situation or would have made Serbs more fearful. It's correct, isn't it, that it would have made Serbs more fearful?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It just made them more cautious because fear is a defensive mechanism in humans. If there were no fear, if there were no pain, humans couldn't live. One of those elements for the preparation of the evil that was in store for us was for us to get organised in order to avoid a repetition of that evil because the memories were very fresh.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender those excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I wonder, really, whether this witness is a proper person through whom these excerpts should be tendered, since he didn't attend the rally and he wasn't asked what he heard about it so that he could actually comment on it other than as any witness who came to this trial can be shown a video and asked to give their general comment. So I don't think that there has been an adequate foundation to admit it through this witness. I would also note that this is a March 1991 rally and the indictment period is October 1991 where the joint criminal enterprise is alleged to have begun, so it's also outside the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour. It was this witness's evidence that the Serbs tried to calm the conflict, or rather, calm the situation and prevent conflict. This video impeaches him on that point. Moreover, it impeaches him on the general point that there was no propaganda related to genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I ask something to be clarified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we assign the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6540, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Having said that it is a propaganda related to genocide, I would like to know whether the position of the Prosecution is that there was no genocide in Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I'd like to turn to the statements of the local SDS in Sanski Most on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P3640.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: E-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You'll see that this is a bulletin issued by the Sanski Most Crisis Staff published on St. Peter's day 1992. St. Peter's day is in July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And the bulletin, we see, was published by the SDS information and promotion centre. I'd like to direct your attention to the editors in chief who are Borislav Savanovic and Dusan Praca. Can you confirm that Mr. Savanovic was the president of the club of SDS deputies of Sanski Most and a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. Which person?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Savanovic was president of the club of SDS deputies?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And if we turn our attention to the associates, we see Oro Nedjelko and you, Boro Tadic. Now the reference to Oro Nedjelko is a reference to Nedjelko Rasula, the Crisis Staff president, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And now I'd like to look at the type of information that you and your colleagues were disseminating.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have English page 3 and B/C/S page 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But did you say this was published by the Crisis Staff, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Yes it's published by the Sanski Most Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do we see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Excuse me, I misspoke. It's published by the SDS of Sanski Most. Thank you for the correction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And it reads: Dear brother Serbs, do you know what our bloodthirsty enemies have been scheming for us? What they had in mind was to gouge our eyes out and carve our insides, hack up our bodies in parts, to rape women and girls in front of their beloved, to circumcise, to destroy our religion, to crush us, just because we happened to be Serbs. And it continues on the same vein, and it says lower down on the page: They have been preparing for a genocide against the Serbs but did not get away with it because we saw what was coming. We warned and prepared our people in time. The leaders of the SDS are resolute in their undertaking to accomplish all that the Serbian people has entrusted them with. So my question, Mr. Tadic, is: Do you agree that this is an example of the propaganda issued by you and your fellow SDS members in Sanski Most to instill fear of non-Serbs in the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: When they talk about the soldiers whom they butchered in a bestial way, well, as far as that is concerned, I was a witness, and I actually drove home this butchered soldier, killed in this way, for him to be buried there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I'm asking you on this point about the propaganda on the topic of genocide, I'm asking you whether this is an example of that type of propaganda. Actually let's move to another example from this article and that is, or rather, from this bulletin, and that's at English page 5 and B/C/S page 4. This is an article by Mr. Rasula, and he states with the -- I'm sorry, if we go to the B/C/S -- or English page 6 and B/C/S page 4. Mr. Rasula states: With the coming of war and the new conditions but still adhering to the goal of creating a Serbian state, the work of the SDS naturally -- followed naturally into a series of duties and actions which served to prepare, organise and provide the Serbian people with the means of guaranteeing its safety in Bosnia and Herzegovina and making it ready for a bitter battle with the other two people, the Muslims, if indeed they are a people, capital letters, they are not, and the Croats, who have forever carried in their genes a sick pathological desire and urge to kill those better and more honest and, do we need to say this, stronger than they are. Mr. Tadic, this is yet another example of the propaganda issued by you and your colleagues to dehumanise non-Serbs; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, still today what Mr. Rasula is writing about is actually being repeated at the Poljud stadium in Split because the entire stadium actually is going out the Ustasha greeting, and this was also repeated -- was repeated in Zagreb at an international match where one of the players was actually saluting the Ustasha salute and the entire stadium responded, and this -- before the face of the entire international community, and the Ustashas are doubtlessly fascists.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you explain in your response to question 7 in relation to what you did to further the Serb authority's goal of protecting the civilian population regardless of their ethnicity, and your contribution was the following: You went to Muslim villages to explain to them that peace should be preserved. You argued that Muslims as Islamicised Serbs would succumb to the evil intentions of the West as they had done before and harm Orthodox Serbs. And you told the Muslims of the original hatred that they had of their own brethren who they deserted by changing their religion that would turn them towards the sly and evil intentions of the West. And you also state that certain extremist Muslims resisted these attempts at persuasion. Mr. Tadic, you will agree that this was not a particularly effective way to protect the non-Serb population of Sanski Most and, in fact, you did nothing to protect them; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
