utterances.text: Well, the truth is always of the essence. Whoever does not speak the truth is actually telling lies. Speaking the truth -- speaking -- saying the truth to those people, actually they could understand by -- from my words by just looking at my face from which emanated love and a desire for peace, they could actually have a change of heart and not do what they had done in 1941, although I'm aware of the fact that only the dear lord can actually make this change in their heart so that they would not hate those from where that nation from which they actually converted to another faith, and that is actually where this essential rift is which was capitalised on by the West in order to dismember a wonderful state, that of Yugoslavia, to bring the Serbs into this position in which today there is practically none of them in Croatia. They have been expelled from Kosovo and Metohija. And the only true shining point, the only good thing in all this is Republika Srpska, which guided by the wisdom of its leadership and by taking democratic measures in an opportune manner and by forming the government and the democratic party it actually precluded something that might have been repeated had we not been prepared. Now, I ask you the question: What would have happened had the Muslims and Croats had the JNA weapons that the Serbs actually had? And I have to tell you that I cried when my assistant, the deputy of the commander -- deputy commander of the battalion, a Muslim, when he left the unit, I cried because I knew that our brotherhood and unity of living together was crumbling, falling apart. This is what the West abused in order to fragmentise a wonderful state into a small fragment so that it could be our master, that it could impose its severe, cruel economic rules of exploitation like it did for centuries with its own colonies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. I'd like to come on to your point about the non-Serb members in your JNA unit. In response to question 2, you say that the JNA's 6th Brigade had a task of preserving peace and preventing escalation of interethnic conflicts and that it controlled the area and provided protection to everyone regardless of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, could we please have P3660. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This, Mr. Tadic, is the wartime record of the 6th Brigade written by Colonel Basara, the commander. I'm interested in page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. And in paragraph 4, it states: On the 3rd of April, 1991, the 6th was transferred to Sanski Most municipality in good order and under a veil of secrecy so that everyone was surprised. Is that a correct reference or should it be to the 3rd of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And it continues: After the brigade came to this area, the Muslims and Croats became afraid while the Serbs heaved a sigh of relief. We had to arm the Serbs quickly and quickly replenish our units, since we, as JNA units, were tasked with preventing interethnic conflicts, i.e., the slaughter of the Serbian people, we could not be seen to be arming the Serbs in public. So this is what you meant by preventing interethnic conflicts, isn't it? The brigade's aim was not the protection of everyone regardless of their ethnicity but, rather, its aim was the protection of the Serbian people; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: To protect the Serbian people against the intentions of those who were planning that meant, at the same time, protecting those who were attempting to do that. The Serbian army ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to your point about -- in the response to question 34, you say in relation to mobilisation from 1991 and until the beginning of the fighting, you say no conscripts who responded to mobilisation were treated differently based on their ethnicity. Could we see page 2 of the English of that and still on the same page and page 4 of the B/C/S. It's on the same passage. And it states, Basara states, we had to resort to trickery to make it possible for us to arm Serbs publicly and legally. A story was invented that the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps ordered that the 6th be promoted from a light to an infantry brigade so that it could have up to 15 battalions and could be additionally mobilised as soon as possible. To prevent Muslims and Croats from joining the brigade, it was said that the brigade would be going to Kupres as long as mobilisation was completed. So in fact, Mr. Tadic, contrary to your statement, Muslims and Croats were actively being prevented from joining your brigade; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: This is a different period altogether. I was talking about the mobilisation of the Yugoslav People's Army, the units of the Yugoslav People's Army, when I was the battalion commander. That was June and July 1991. By organised political activity of the SDA and the HDZ, the Muslims and Croats were leaving the units, and the crying, when I cried when what I referred to before, I was really deeply saddened by the fact that my deputy commander was leaving me and the unit. That was in September 1991. Namely, the leadership of the Muslims and Croats wanted their conscripts not to do service, not to go to the Yugoslav People's Army because their plan was that there should be no Yugoslavia. That is why -- that is how they made the army Serbian, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: In response to question 2, you say -- you discuss the events that were happening at the end of May and you say, all this indicated that Muslims and Croats illegally armed, although some responded to the 1991 mobilisation, they were increasingly leaving the unit. Now, it's true, isn't it, that Muslims and Croats who were leaving the unit at the end of May 1992 were leaving the unit because of its attacks on the Muslim population in that area?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this was not at all about Muslims and Croats leaving because that was a year -- half a year before. That was in the summer and autumn of 1991. They actually obeyed their own leaderships, both the Muslims and the Croats, they just wouldn't and did not respond to the mobilisation, to the call-up. And those who still believed in Yugoslavia, a little at least, they also left and that is how the Serb army was created.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P3662.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seventeen, line 17, it is stated "yes, yes, but," and what he actually said, "then." He didn't say "yes, yes," "da, da," he said "tada" which is "then," at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, this is a document dated the 31st of May, 1992. It's a 1st Krajina Corps command report to the SRBiH army Main Staff. And could we see page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S, please. And I'd like to focus your attention on section 5(b) halfway through it, and it states: After the actions in Kozarac, Kljuc and Sanski Most, some conscripts of Muslim nationality have asked to be released from their units. They expressed their dissatisfaction with the massive destruction of their towns. Now, it's true, isn't it, that Muslims in the Sanski Most area left the JNA because of the JNA's massive destruction of their towns?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: These were just several soldiers who joined this young officer who was the only one who remained till the end and he was in Jasenovac and then came to Sanski Most. So we are talking about just a small number of soldiers, I cannot say exactly, between 10 and 20 soldiers were in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we will come back to the issue of the massive destruction of Muslim towns. But, briefly, you stayed in -- or you refer to the corridor through Posavina in your answers to questions 5 and 6. This corridor was -- or the establishment of this corridor was a key strategic goal for the VRS from its establishment. From the establishment of the VRS, the Posavina corridor was a key strategic goal; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: That is the essence of the evil, which in quotation marks, the international community, and I say the West, actually inflicted on us. It was all well thought beforehand in order to place the Serbs in a disadvantaged position. That is why sanctions were imposed on Serbs, that is why Serbs were bombed, that is why Serbian babies died because they could not get oxygen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but my question is, isn't it correct that it was a key strategic goal of the VRS to establish the Posavina corridor?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: That is what I'm saying. So those who actually created this strife in Yugoslavia, those, they who planned the war, they are the ones who actually charged us with the task of having to survive, to breach this corridor of life in order to be able to reach food, medicaments and everything which is necessary for a human being to survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, do you agree that the establishment of the Posavina corridor was a key strategic military goal for the VRS, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. That is precisely what the problem is. In line 6 and 7, an entire sentence -- the witness said the entire Krajina was cut off and there was no -- there is no reference to that sentence. The entire Krajina was cut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm having said that, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But this is the intention of those who actually planned to destroy our country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic I'd like to look at the operations that were conducted in pursuit of that goal, and specifically the operations that the 6th Brigade and your battalion were involved in. Now, we've seen that you arrived in Sanski Most with your unit on the 3rd of April. It's correct, isn't it, that on the 19th of April, together with the TO and other Serb forces, the 6th Brigade conducted an armed attack on the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Then, and I said this before, I came from the military hospital in Sarajevo where I had been from 17 March until 2 April, and after getting just a little bit of treatment, I was no longer a battalion commander, I was assistant brigade commander for morale and religious affairs. And that's why I went touring Muslim villages to tell people to save peace. And later, I went --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: As assistant brigade commander for morale and religious affairs, were you aware of the military operations that the 6th Brigade was engaged in?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Superficially. I didn't know anything in detail because I wasn't still quite well. I had just been discharged from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Okay, well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. The witness didn't say "I didn't know anything in detail." He said "I didn't know in detail."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any difference. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Concerns credibility of witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the 6th Brigade was involved in the attack on the municipality building on the 19th of April, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was in Palanka and I was not au courant at all. I was sick and far from there, and I was not privy to the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer, you're saying that you did not know that on the 19th of April, your brigade was involved in an attack on the municipality building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I heard about that later, but I did not take part in it and I wasn't even informed during those few days because we were cut off. We were in Palanka, that's 25 kilometres to the west. We were not in a position to know the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Were you also informed that the 6th Brigade was involved in the take-over of power in Kljuc from the 7th to the 10th of May? Were you informed of that?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I know they went to Kljuc. I know that much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Is that a yes, they were involved in the take-over of power in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It's the place where soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army were ambushed and killed by organised Muslim paramilitary units, and we, as the only armed force, up until the recognition of Yugoslavia by that West who was planning its break-up, the Muslims and Croats had been secretly preparing for that, that's why they attacked convoys and columns and provoked conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I believe the ambushes to which you're referring, purported ambushes, happened at the end of May. I'm asking you about incidents at the start of May. I'm asking you to confirm whether, from the 7th to 10th of May, 1992, the 6th Brigade was involved in the take-over of power in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I cannot really say that it was at that time, really not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's talk about their later activities. Can you confirm that from the 25th of May to the 4th of June, the 6th Brigade was involved in a comprehensive operation to mop up the terrain and disarm non-Serbs in Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I know work had been done to seize illegally owned weapons from Muslims and Croats, and that went rather peacefully except that occasionally incidents happened. One soldier was killed in Trnovo village. I said that in my statement, at the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's talk about these rather peaceful operations to which you refer. The comprehensive operation to mop up the terrain - for the parties' reference that's P3663 - started with a joint JNA-TO attack on Mahala and the surrounding settlements on the 26th of May. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, I was in Palanka at the time and I still wasn't well enough. I hadn't completely recovered. And the assistant for moral guidance and religious affairs was not obliged to be present except on the commander's orders, not at discussions of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: While you may not have been present, did you hear, as this Trial Chamber has heard, that Serb soldiers forced Mahala residents to gather at a training ground and then the village was shelled by the 6th Brigade, businesses were blown up and house burned down selectively? Did you hear of that?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: All sorts of things could be heard, but I didn't take part in that and I cannot talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, a witness in the Brdjanin case, Mr. Besim Islamcevic places you in Mahala and says that you were one of the ones going from house to house in Mahala saying which ones should be burned down and which ones not.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: No. Never in my life had that thought crossed my mind, let alone that I would have done it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, the operation at Mahala which you have -- well, let me -- let me ask you to clarify: Did you at the time hear of the operation at Mahala?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I did, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And were you aware, or can you confirm, that the operation involved the detention of thousands of unarmed civilians, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I heard later that in order to protect them from combat, they were placed in some sort of gym or hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's correct, isn't it, that as part of that operation, thousands of unarmed civilians were detained?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I could not confirm the number. I know there was a certain number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, can you confirm that many civilians were killed in this operation?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time -- is that -- are you saying -- is it your evidence that you were unaware that civilians were killed in this operation?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I can't recall now. I can't remember at all that I was aware of it, even a few days later, that some people had been killed because I did come to Sanski Most later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So just to clarify, what date did you come to Sanski Most on?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I can't say that. I don't know. When the situation calmed down, I was not able to go to work through Gornji and Donji Kamengrad because the Muslims were there and it was very risky to go to work that way because at that time, that was the crossing. I was assistant commander for moral guidance at the time, and about to join the Secretariat for National Defence, so that was the transition period in which I was not informed well enough, nor did I have firsthand knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And yet you're informed well enough to sit here and testify before this Trial Chamber that the operations were conducted peacefully when there is evidence before the Trial Chamber that this brutal operation on Mahala in which your brigade was involved, involved the detention of thousands of civilians and the killing of numerous unarmed civilians.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I only know that a few soldiers were killed, one of them was even slaughtered, butchered, and I personally organised his funeral.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, the 6th Brigade operations continued after Mahala and they were involved in the attacks on the villages of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: That's when that thing happened with those soldiers. I believe that was the end of May, I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And in answer to question 39, you state that the 6th Brigade advocated that members of the unit should be punished if they committed crimes against non-Serbs. Mr. Tadic, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that, on the 31st of May, members of 6th Brigade unit entered Begici, near Vrhpolje, rounded up its inhabitants, took the men to Vrhpolje bridge, killing some along the way, and then at the bridge the men were forced to jump off and were shot at as they did. And at least 28 Muslim men were killed on that day. Now, no one was ever charged for this incident, were they?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, what about an incident on the same date that involved the shooting of unarmed civilians in Hrustovo where the 6th Brigade soldiers were involved in the shooting of women and children who were taking shelter in a garage in Hrustovo? Was anyone charged for that incident?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm what happened either, nor can I confirm whether something had been done about it, but I know that in that specific case, some Serbs, beginning with Kajtez, were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's talk about Kajtez. There is evidence before the Trial Chamber that he was taken into custody by the Banja Luka military court on the 7th of December, 1992, for the killing of seven Croatian villagers. And from the beginning, he and his co-accused admitted to the murder, and yet their detention was suspended less than one month later, on the 22nd of January, 1993 - for the parties' reference that's P3621 - and the defendants stated -- or the record stated that the defendants stated that they wanted to return to their unit. Now, a military court releasing a confessed murderer to return to his unit doesn't suggest a desire to properly bring him to justice, does it?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I really don't know the truth about that. Throughout that time, I was working on mobilisation and commandeering of resources. I was not involved in that part of the brigade's work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And yet it's your position, it's your evidence before this Trial Chamber, that the brigade advocated that all members of the unit should be tried if they committed crimes against non-Serbs. Now, the civilian authorities and the 6th Brigade leadership were aware of the crimes committed against non-Serbs by Kajtez, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: While I was assistant for moral guidance and religious affairs, whenever I spoke I told our troops too that every crime will have to be answered for, first before God and then before people. They should be concerned more for their soul than their bodies. I never supported and never said anything different.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's your evidence, Mr. Tadic, that the brigade advocated that all crimes against non-Serbs be prosecuted. I'd like to direct your

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, this is a letter of the SDS Sanski Most municipal board sent to the Banja Luka military court dated the 10th of September, 1993, and I should say just to clarify that the military court ordered detention for Mr. Kajtez again on the 9th of July, 1993. And this letter if we will see from the signature --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'm wondering if we should go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Out of an abundance of caution we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Yes, and this will be the final document for today. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So if we can look at the signatures on this letter we'll see that it is signed by Vlado Verkes, who was the president of the Sanski Most SDS municipal board and a Crisis Staff member, and Captain Ostoja Cukov, who was commander of the 4th Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade. If you could go back to the first page, the third paragraph of this letter, and this also responds to Mr. Karadzic's question, states that Kajtez was a member of the 6th Krajina Brigade, he took part in the fighting in Sanski Most and neighbouring municipalities in the corridor and on other battlefields. It states that in carrying out combat tasks, he showed exceptional courage and determination as a soldier of the Army of Republika Srpska, and in -- at the conclusion of the document in the next page, it states, the tragedy of the Serbian people and his family in the Second World War and in this war have left visible traces on Kajtez's mental state and we would like you to take this into account and pass fair judgement on him. So, Mr. Tadic, it's not true, is it, that the brigade advocated that crimes against non-Serbs be punished? The truth is that the leadership in the brigade lobbied for Kajtez, a self-confessed killer of Muslims and Croats, to be treated leniently. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It's enough to look at this explanation, how many members of his family were killed by Ustashas. Obviously that can leave serious consequences on the psyche, not that I'm justifying anything like that, but because I have no direct knowledge, I can give no further comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, in fact, contrary to your evidence, despite your claim to have no direct knowledge now, contrary to your evidence and your statement, Kajtez was not tried by Republika Srpska courts but was released on the 14th of March, 1995. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only know that there was a trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kajtez [sic], there was a trial in 2006 by the BiH state court but you're not aware of any previous trial, are you?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I heard that he had confessed and that court proceedings had started, and that's what I said in my statement. We were trying to inflict as little evil on others because any evil you do unto others you do unto yourself, in fact. That's how I always acted and what I always thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, do you agree that Mr. Verkes and Captain Cukov sent this letter to the military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see they did. And they tried to mitigate his guilt by the mental stress caused by what had been done to his nearest and dearest in World War II.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we continue tomorrow, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, we will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00, but I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you are giving evidence here. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of December, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
